title: Level 1 – Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Mental Health Care
intro: Welcome to GNPS Program 8 - Compassionate Mental Health Care. Mental health nursing is grounded in respect, empathy, safety and partnership. Nurses encounter people experiencing emotional distress, mental illness, substance-related problems and behavioural change in every healthcare setting, not only specialist services. This level is designed around the mental health capabilities expected within national nursing education programs and by nursing regulatory bodies across different countries. It develops the essential knowledge, assessment skills and professional behaviours required to provide person-centred, recovery-oriented and safe care. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Explain mental health, mental illness and recovery-oriented practice Build a therapeutic nurse-person relationship Conduct a basic mental health assessment Use effective therapeutic communication Recognise common mood, anxiety, psychotic and substance-use disorders Identify risk of self-harm, suicide, aggression and deterioration Apply least restrictive and safe interventions Understand common psychotropic medicines and monitoring needs Practise ethically, culturally and professionally Mental distress may be hidden behind physical symptoms, withdrawal, agitation or changes in behaviour. A calm conversation, direct risk assessment and timely escalation can prevent harm and help a person feel heard rather than judged. By the end of Level 1, you should be able to provide compassionate, recovery-oriented mental health nursing care, complete a person-centred assessment and respond safely to common mental health risks within your scope of practice. Level 1 - Qualified Nurse

sections.title: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing

content.text: Mental health nursing recognises the person beyond diagnosis. Recovery does not always mean the complete absence of symptoms. It may mean living a meaningful, hopeful and self-directed life while managing ongoing challenges. Nurses support recovery by listening, respecting choice, identifying strengths and reducing stigma.
Learning outcomes
Explain mental health, mental illness and wellbeing Describe recovery-oriented practice
Identify factors influencing mental health Apply non-judgemental and strengths-based care

Mental Health and Wellbeing Mental health exists on a continuum and is influenced by biological, psychological, social, cultural and environmental factors. A person may experience distress without a diagnosed disorder, while another may live well with a long-term condition.
Recovery Orientation Recovery-oriented care supports hope, choice, identity, meaning and participation. The person is an active partner rather than a passive recipient of treatment.
Stigma and Discrimination Stigma may prevent people from seeking help and can affect employment, housing, relationships and physical healthcare. Nurses challenge stigmatising language and attitudes.
Holistic Care Mental and physical health are interconnected. Sleep, nutrition, pain, medication, substance use, trauma, relationships and social conditions should all be considered.

Mr Khan has recurrent depression and says, "I am more than this illness." The nurse asks about his goals, strengths and what has helped previously. Together they identify sleep, social contact and return to study as important recovery goals alongside treatment.
Key learning points
See the person, not only the diagnosis Support hope, choice and strengths
Challenge stigma in everyday practice Include physical, social and cultural needs in care

The therapeutic relationship is central to mental health nursing. It is purposeful, time-limited and focused on the person's needs. Trust develops through consistency, empathy, honesty and clear boundaries.
Learning outcomes
Use active listening and empathy Apply therapeutic communication techniques
Recognise non-therapeutic responses Maintain professional boundaries
Active Listening Active listening includes attentive posture, silence, reflection, clarification and summarising. It communicates respect and helps the person organise thoughts and feelings.
Therapeutic Responses Open questions, validation and exploration encourage communication. False reassurance, judgement, arguing and immediate advice can close discussion.
Responding to Distress When a person is anxious, withdrawn or suspicious, the nurse should use calm, simple language and avoid overwhelming questions. Trust may need to develop gradually.

Professional Boundaries Boundaries protect both the person and nurse. Nurses should avoid secrecy, personal financial involvement, inappropriate self-disclosure and relationships outside the therapeutic role.

A woman says, "Nothing will ever get better." Instead of saying, "You will be fine," the nurse responds, "It sounds as though things feel hopeless right now. Can you tell me more about what has been happening?" This validates distress and opens further assessment.
Key learning points
Listen before offering solutions Use empathy rather than false reassurance
Adapt communication to the person's state Maintain clear and respectful boundaries

sections.title: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions

content.text: A mental health assessment combines the person's story, observed behaviour, mental state, physical health and current risks. The assessment should be collaborative and should not reduce the person to a checklist.
Learning outcomes
Conduct a basic mental state examination Assess mood, thought, perception and cognition
Recognise common mental health conditions Identify changes requiring further review
Mental State Examination The mental state examination considers appearance, behaviour, speech, mood, affect, thought form and content, perception, cognition, insight and judgement.

Mood and Anxiety Disorders Depression may involve low mood, loss of interest, sleep or appetite change and hopelessness. Mania may involve elevated mood, reduced sleep, rapid speech and risky behaviour. Anxiety can range from persistent worry to panic.

Psychotic Disorders Psychosis may involve hallucinations, delusions, disorganised thought and reduced functioning. Nurses should assess the meaning, impact and safety implications without arguing about the belief.

Substance Use and Cognitive Change Substance intoxication or withdrawal can affect behaviour and risk. Delirium, dementia and depression may present differently and require careful assessment, especially in older adults.

A patient reports hearing a voice telling him to harm himself. The nurse asks directly what the voice says, whether he intends to act, what access he has to means and what helps him resist. The response is calm, respectful and focused on safety.
Key learning points
Use observation and conversation together Ask directly about hallucinations and risk
Distinguish psychiatric symptoms from possible delirium or substance effects
Document findings objectively

Mental health crises may involve suicidal thoughts, self-harm, aggression, severe withdrawal, panic, mania or psychosis. The nurse must protect safety while preserving dignity and using the least restrictive effective response.
Learning outcomes
Identify immediate mental health risks Use de-escalation and least restrictive care
Respond appropriately to suicidal or aggressive behaviour Recognise important psychotropic medication risks

Suicide and Self-Harm Risk Direct questions about thoughts, plan, intent, means, past behaviour and protective factors do not create suicidal ideas. Immediate safety planning and escalation are required when risk is high.
De-escalation A calm tone, respectful distance, clear choices, reduced stimulation and attention to unmet needs may reduce escalation. Staff safety and exit access should be maintained.
Least Restrictive Practice Restriction, restraint or seclusion should only be used according to law and policy when less restrictive measures are insufficient to manage serious immediate risk.

Psychotropic Medicines Antidepressants, mood stabilisers, antipsychotics and anxiolytics require monitoring. Serious reactions include serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, severe withdrawal and excessive sedation.

A patient becomes increasingly agitated, pacing and shouting. The nurse reduces noise, maintains a safe distance, speaks calmly, offers choices and calls for support early. When the patient states an intention to attack another person, the team follows the emergency safety plan.
Key learning points
Ask directly about suicide and violence risk Use de-escalation early
Choose the least restrictive safe response Monitor for serious medication toxicity and adverse effects

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 8 - Level 1, you have developed the foundational knowledge and practical skills required to provide recovery-oriented care, communicate therapeutically, complete a mental health assessment and respond safely to common disorders and crises. These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse, where the focus expands to complex risk, law, medication and multidisciplinary practice.
